title: Geometry contribution to sound attenuation in double-Weyl semimetals
authors: Varsha Subramanyan, Shi-Zeng Lin, Avadh Saxena
abstract: The axial coupling of strain to the nodes of the simple Weyl semimetals leads to anomalous contributions to sound attenuation in such materials. However, in double Weyl semimetals, there is no such axial coupling. Strain instead couples as a symmetry-breaking director field that deforms the Fermi surface around each Weyl node. In this work, we show that absence of axial coupling in double Weyl semimetals implies a very different mechanism of relaxation due to sound. The deformed geometry of the Fermi surface is the only source of sound attenuation under these conditions. Thus, we identify a geometric contribution to sound attenuation in double Weyl semimetals that is entirely absent in simple Weyl semimetals.
summary: This paper theoretically analyzes sound attenuation in double-Weyl semimetals, demonstrating that the damping mechanism is purely geometric due to Fermi surface deformation. This contrasts sharply with simple Weyl semimetals, where a different axial coupling dominates. The findings establish a new diagnostic tool for characterizing topological electronic states using acoustic measurements.
main_problem: The study investigates the mechanism by which sound waves cause energy attenuation in double-Weyl semimetals (DWSMs) compared to simple Weyl semimetals (WSMs). The core goal is to identify a novel, purely geometric contribution to this damping.
main_result: In DWSMs, sound attenuation is dominated entirely by the deformation of the Fermi surface geometry due to strain. This mechanism is fundamentally different from WSMs because the characteristic axial coupling present in simple WSMs vanishes in the double-Weyl case.
method: The authors employ a semi-classical approach using the Boltzmann transport equation to calculate the rate of change of energy ($Q$) induced by dynamic strain, leading to the attenuation coefficient ($\Gamma$).
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a double-Weyl semimetal described by a low-energy Hamiltonian modified by strain. The analysis compares this behavior against simple Weyl semimetals and utilizes concepts like the quantum geometric tensor ($g_{ij}$) to quantify strain effects.
key_observables: Sound attenuation coefficient ($\Gamma$), energy shift ($\delta E$), and the inter-node scattering rate ($\Lambda(E)$).
important_parameters: Strain tensor components ($u_{ij}$), Grüneisen parameter ($\gamma$), sound frequency ($\omega$), and Fermi surface geometry parameters.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes slow-moving sound waves ($\omega	au^* \ll 1$) and relies on semi-classical approximations derived from the Boltzmann transport equation. The dominance of geometric effects is assumed over other coupling mechanisms.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the change in Fermi surface geometry under strain, showing transitions from unstrained to nematic shapes during sound passage for a DWSM.
paper_structure: The paper develops by first establishing the general framework for calculating energy loss due to strain. It then contrasts the coupling mechanisms between simple WSMs (axial coupling) and DWSMs (geometric deformation). Finally, it derives the specific geometric contribution to $\Gamma$ unique to DWSMs.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed theoretical link between crystal lattice dynamics (sound waves/strain) and topological electronic structure (Weyl nodes), offering insights into how geometry dictates transport properties in novel quantum materials.
